title: Repeated Music Listening Modulates Beta Band Oscillatory Activity and Autobiographical Memory in Older Adults
content:
Listening to autobiographically salient (ABS) music (songs connected to one's past) elicits distinct oscillatory activity from familiar (FAM) music (recognized but lacking personal significance), yet the effects of repeated ABS listening remain unclear. We measured autobiographical memory and music-evoked oscillatory activity in 33 healthy older adults before and after a 2-week ABS intervention. Autobiographical memory subscores (reliving, narrative coherence) increased and parietal beta desynchronization decreased for ABS relative to FAM music.


ABSTRACT

Music listening is increasingly used as a nonpharmacological intervention to elicit memory retrieval. Evidence suggests that listening to autobiographically salient (ABS) music (i.e., songs associated with significant people, places, events) generates distinct neural oscillatory activity compared with familiar (FAM) music (i.e., songs that are recognized but lack personal significance). We assessed the effects of a 2-week (20 min/day) ABS music-listening intervention on behavioral autobiographical memory and music-evoked oscillatory activity in 33 healthy older adults. Listening experiences documented throughout the intervention were also examined. Following the intervention, reliving and narrative coherence subscores on the Autobiographical Recollection Test increased significantly. Time-frequency analysis revealed condition-dependent modulation over time, characterized by reduced left parietal beta desynchronization in response to ABS compared to FAM music. A repeated-measures correlation revealed within-participant associations between parietal beta power during ABS music listening and reliving subscores. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four themes characterizing the listening experience: emotional responses; autobiographical reflection; active engagement; and evolving responses to ABS music over time. Together, these results suggest that a 2-week ABS music-listening intervention is associated with increases in behavioral autobiographical memory, modulations in music-evoked oscillations, and multifaceted listening experiences in older adults. These findings may inform future music-based interventions for memory disorders.
